Thad Kittredge framed houses for other builders for fifteen years, then started his own company with one truck and one rule: write the number down before anyone picks up a hammer. Seventeen years later the truck is a fleet and the rule is the contract.

Every carpenter and superintendent on the crew is our own employee, background-checked and covered by workers’ comp. If a frame or foundation we built fails within ten years, we come back and fix it, it says so in every contract.
One truck, one framing crew and a rule: write the number down first.
Licensed BC-A in Tennessee, and the first additions under our own name.
A 3,400 sq ft house in Farragut, and the 1-2-10 warranty in writing.
Garland joined, and offices, clinics and cafés became the fourth line of work.
Six job sites at a time across Knox and Blount County, 4.9 on Google.
Every project type: Knoxville, Farragut, Powell, Hardin Valley
Additions, remodels and homes: Maryville, Oak Ridge, Lenoir City, Seymour

When a family outgrows a house, the first instinct is to look at listings. Before you do, put both options on one page.
On a $450,000 house, agent commissions, closing costs on both ends, moving and the small repairs buyers ask for add up to around $45,000. That money buys nothing you can live in.

A 450 sq ft primary suite starts around $158,000 in our cost guide. A second story runs about $290 per square foot. Both add value to the house you already own, and you keep the neighbors, the school and the commute.

If the lot is too small, the setbacks leave no room, or the house needs a new foundation as well, moving can be the better answer. We will tell you that at the site walk; it costs you nothing to hear it.

Most of the lots left inside Knox County are not flat. That is not bad news. A slope can give you a walkout lower level with daylight and a view, often for less per square foot than the floors above it.

Expect $58,000 and up for a walkout basement: excavation, poured walls, waterproofing, a drain to daylight and framing. Steeper lots need retaining walls, which we price separately once the engineer has seen the soil report.

East Tennessee has clay that holds water and limestone that turns up where you least want it. We order two soil borings before the foundation design, about $2,400 with the survey, because finding rock with an excavator costs far more.
A long, steep drive can cost as much as a kitchen. We walk the drive route on the first visit and put a number on it before you buy the lot, if you ask us early enough.

How to read a builder’s estimate, line by line
Allowances, exclusions, contingency and markup: what each line means and which ones decide the final invoice.
Questions about your own project? Call (865) 555-0142 and a builder answers.
Two estimates for the same house can be $80,000 apart and both be honest. The difference is usually in four places, and once you know where to look you can compare any two builders in an evening.

An allowance is a placeholder for something you have not chosen yet. A $6,000 tile allowance and a $14,000 tile allowance make the same house look very different on paper. Ask for every allowance in dollars and compare them side by side.

Read what is not included before what is. Driveways, landscaping, appliances and utility fees are the usual suspects. If one estimate includes them and the other does not, the cheaper one is not cheaper.

We show both. Contingency covers what nobody can see before work starts, and unused contingency comes back to you. Markup is our overhead and profit, a fixed percentage written on the estimate, so you never wonder where it is hiding.

Most kitchens we remodel keep their footprint. The difference between a $68,000 kitchen and a $115,000 kitchen is usually not walls, it is what goes on them.

Cabinets take a third of the budget. Counters, the backsplash and the plumbing fixtures take another quarter. Labor for demolition, electrical and plumbing changes is the steadiest part of the number.

We set allowances from the showroom, not from a catalog. Before the estimate is final, you spend one afternoon with Liesl choosing cabinets, counters and tile at real prices, and those prices become the allowances.
If you choose under the allowance, the difference comes off the invoice. If you choose over it, you see the new number on a change order before anything is ordered.

Every few weeks someone asks us for a price per square foot before they have a lot, a plan or a budget. It is a fair question, so here is the honest answer from our own contracts.

Our last 31 custom homes in Knox and Blount County landed between $238 and $455 per square foot of heated space. Standard finishes on a level lot sit around $245. Premium finishes, site-finished hardwood, quartz and spray foam, sit around $325. Architect-designed houses with steel, big glass and complex roofs start near $410.

The lot moves it first. A sloped lot can add a walkout level for less than an addition costs, but the excavation, retaining and drainage run $40,000 to $90,000. Long driveways, septic systems and rock under the footings all show up here.
Finishes move it second. Cabinets, counters, flooring and plumbing fixtures are written as allowances in our estimates, so you can see exactly which choices push the number up.
Three lines first estimates leave out

Utility connections and tap fees, which can reach $15,000 on a rural lot. Landscaping past final grade. And a contingency for the things nobody can see before digging. Ours are on the estimate, with a dollar figure next to each.

The short version: the contract price you signed is the price on the final invoice, plus only the change orders you signed. The rest is detail.

The itemized estimate becomes the contract price. If we find something nobody could see, rot behind a wall or rock under a footing, we stop and you approve a written change order with its price before we carry on.

Fixtures and finishes you have not chosen yet are written as allowances in dollars. Choose under the allowance and the difference comes off the invoice; choose over it and you see the new number before we order.
A 10% deposit at signing, then draws tied to inspections, never to dates: foundation, framing, drywall, substantial completion. We hold back 5% until the punch list is done.
One year on workmanship and finishes, two years on plumbing, electrical and HVAC systems, ten years on the structural frame and foundation, from the date of substantial completion.
Cancel free until the permit is pulled. After that you pay for design, permit fees and any materials already ordered, at cost, with receipts.
